projects.name: StudyHub
projects.description: A full-stack web application built with a team of six that helps college students organize courses, assignments, deadlines, and study resources in one dashboard. I led the frontend and reviewed and merged code as part of the team's pull request workflow.

details.tagline: A team-built student organization platform with Google sign-in, where I led the frontend design and helped review and merge team code
details.problem: The goal was to give college students one simple place to manage their academic responsibilities instead of tracking courses, deadlines, and study materials across separate tools, while working with a team of six on a shared codebase using a professional Git workflow.
features: Google authentication using Auth.js and Google OAuth
Personal dashboard highlighting upcoming assignments
Create, view, edit, and delete courses, assignments, and study resources
Assignments organized by course with due dates and completion tracking
Study resources saved as external links and text notes tied to each course
Reusable component library I built, including cards, buttons, links, forms, header, and navigation bar
Styled login, onboarding, and main application pages
Responsive interface for desktop, tablet, and mobile using Tailwind CSS
Production deployment on Vercel
details.challenges: The biggest challenge was collaborating with six developers building different features on separate branches in one GitHub repository. We kept the codebase stable with a strict workflow of feature branches, focused pull requests, and teammate reviews. I took an active role by reviewing pull requests, checking that branches worked correctly before merging, and merging several of them myself. Another challenge was Google authentication, since connecting Google OAuth required correctly configuring credentials, environment variables, and redirect URIs for both local development and the deployed site before login worked reliably.
details.learning: Gained hands-on experience building the frontend of a production-style application with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. Strengthened my ability to design consistent, reusable, and accessible UI components across an entire application. Learned how professional teams collaborate through branching, pull requests, code review, and merging, and gained a practical understanding of how OAuth authentication connects a frontend to a backend.

projects.name: Sacrament Meeting Planner
projects.description: A full-stack Next.js application, built week by week in a web development course, that lets bishopric leaders plan sacrament meeting agendas and lets members view current and past programs.

details.tagline: A full-stack meeting planner with a live PostgreSQL database, protected admin tools, and URL-driven search
details.problem: The goal was to build a real application that helps ward leaders plan and review sacrament meeting programs, including leadership, announcements, hymns, musical numbers, speakers, and prayers, while members can view current and past programs. Each week added a new layer of professional web development to the same codebase.
features: Typed data models in TypeScript for meetings and their program details
Live PostgreSQL database on Neon, so meeting data persists across restarts and deployments
Public and admin sections separated with Next.js route groups, each with its own layout and loading states
URL-based search by speaker, presiding, conducting, or meeting type, with pagination at five meetings per page
Create, edit, and delete meetings through Server Actions with accessible server-side form validation
Graceful error handling for failed operations and missing records
Site-wide metadata defaults, custom page metadata, and an Open Graph image for link previews
Responsive Tailwind CSS styling, optimized fonts and images, and deployment on Vercel
Authentication with Auth.js credentials and hashed passwords, with protected admin routes that redirect signed-out users to the login page
details.challenges: The hardest part was working across every layer of the application at once: frontend styling, middleware, authentication and authorization, database queries, and validation. Each layer had to work correctly with the others, so a problem in one place often showed up somewhere else. Making error.tsx and not-found.tsx work was especially tricky, since I had to learn how Next.js scopes them by route segment so that failed operations and missing records were handled gracefully across many pages instead of just one. I also spent a lot of time making sure data was fetched from the database correctly and that user input was validated on the server, so only the content the application expected was ever saved. Authentication also worked locally but failed after deployment, because the secrets live in a local environment file that is never committed. Reading the Vercel logs pointed to a missing AUTH_SECRET, and adding it as a production environment variable and redeploying fixed it.
details.learning: Gained hands-on experience building and deploying a full-stack application with the Next.js App Router, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL. Strengthened my understanding of Server Actions, server-side validation, route groups, URL-driven state, authentication, and metadata. Most importantly, learned how to grow one application week by week without breaking what already worked.

details.tagline: A full-stack service management application built progressively with Node.js, Express, EJS, and PostgreSQL
details.problem: The goal was to transform an existing web application into a fully dynamic, database-driven system while progressively learning and implementing the core concepts of backend web development. Each week introduced new functionality through learning activities, team development, and individual assignments, culminating in a final feature that integrated concepts from across the course.
features: Server-side rendered pages using Node.js, Express.js, and EJS
Relational PostgreSQL database for organizations, service projects, categories, and users
MVC architecture separating routes, controllers, models, and views
Full CRUD functionality for organizations, projects, and categories
Many-to-many relationships between service projects and categories
User registration, login, logout, and session management
Password hashing and secure user authentication using bcrypt
Role-based authorization middleware for protecting administrator functionality
Server-side and client-side form validation with user feedback
User dashboard displaying volunteer projects and account information
Middleware for flash messages and request-based application behavior
Production deployment using Render
details.challenges: The primary challenge was continuously expanding an existing application without breaking the functionality that had already been developed. As new concepts were introduced, the application had to evolve from basic server-side routing into a structured MVC application with database relationships, CRUD operations, validation, sessions, authentication, and role-based authorization. Managing the flow of data between routes, controllers, models, SQL queries, and EJS templates required careful debugging and a stronger understanding of how the different layers of a backend application interact.
details.learning: Developed a strong foundation in backend web development and learned how frontend applications connect to servers, databases, and persistent user data. Strengthened my understanding of Node.js, Express.js, EJS, PostgreSQL, SQL, MVC architecture, middleware, authentication, authorization, sessions, validation, and deployment. Most importantly, gained experience progressively developing and maintaining a larger application while learning how individual backend concepts work together as part of a complete system.

projects.name: B.R.A.N.D.O.N.
projects.description: Earth's last line of defense against descending alien fleets. A Galaga-inspired Pygame arcade shooter built with custom-designed ships, four-direction movement, and a rebalanced difficulty curve.

details.tagline: Brutal Retaliation Against Nefarious Descending Orbital Nuisances: one pilot, three ships, and a planet to protect
details.problem: The goal was to defend Earth from an endless invasion of descending aliens, or more accurately, to build a complete 2D arcade shooter in Pygame with escalating levels, lives, and scoring. I built the core by following Python Crash Course, then spent the rest of the project making it my own.
features: Fleets of hostile aliens that sweep across and down the screen, getting faster with every wave
Three-ship mission structure with a live scoreboard and a high score tracked during each play session
Four-direction ship movement, extended beyond the book's left and right controls for a more Galaga-like feel
Alternate WASD controls alongside the arrow keys, so left-handed pilots can defend Earth too
Custom ship and alien designs I created from scratch in Adobe Illustrator and exported as PNG sprites
Scalable space background inspired by Regular Show that crops to the window instead of warping
Rebalanced difficulty with slower speeds and a smaller starting fleet so players can last longer and chase high scores
details.challenges: The most important battles were fought on the home front. Getting smooth movement meant understanding the difference between pressing and holding a key, then adapting that same logic for up and down movement. Tuning the game was another fight, since both the starting speed and the speed increase per level needed repeated testing to land in the sweet spot between boring and impossible. The background initially warped on different window sizes, so I fixed it by cropping the image to the window rather than stretching it. The biggest effort was the custom ships, which meant planning, brainstorming, designing in Illustrator, tweaking, resizing, and exporting each one before it looked right in the game.
details.learning: Strengthened my understanding of Python, Pygame, event-driven input, and organizing a larger project across multiple files. Gained experience tuning game difficulty and modifying an existing codebase without breaking it. Most importantly, learned how much ownership comes from going beyond a tutorial, since designing my own art and adding new mechanics turned a guided project into one that is truly mine.

projects.name: Falling Sand Simulator
projects.description: A real-time physics simulation where sand falls, bubbles drift upward, and rocks stay put, built with object-oriented programming and class inheritance for a university programming course.

details.tagline: A real-time particle simulation of sand, bubbles, and rocks built on object-oriented design and inheritance
details.problem: The goal was to practice object-oriented programming and inheritance by building a particle simulation on top of a custom grid class, where every kind of particle shares core behavior but follows its own rules of motion.
features: Custom Grid class with bounds-checked access, validated construction from nested lists, and independent copies
Shared Particle base class that tracks position and grid reference for every particle type
Sand, Bubble, and Rock subclasses that each define their own physics
Sand that falls and slides diagonally around obstacles, and bubbles that rise the same way in reverse
Diagonal movement rules that stop particles from squeezing through gaps between blocked cells
Functions to add and remove particles at any location, keeping the grid and the master particle list in sync
Two-pass update order that keeps falling sand and rising bubbles from leaving gaps in a column
Whimsical bubbles: an optional extension from the assignment, where bubbles drift sideways and rise lazily using weighted random choices, a deliberate idle chance, and fallback moves when blocked
Run through a provided Pygame interface (adapted from a Stanford CS106A project) with click-to-draw and erase controls
details.challenges: The hardest part was reasoning about diagonal movement. A particle cannot slip between two blocked cells, which means checking a neighboring cell in addition to the destination, and it took sketching the grid by hand to see which cell that was. Update order was the other tricky piece: moving particles in a single pass left visible gaps in falling columns, so sand and bubbles needed separate passes in opposite directions. Keeping the grid and the particle list consistent whenever particles were added or removed was a third, since a mismatch produces particles that vanish from the screen but keep moving. For the bubble extension, I had to tune the probabilities so that a blocked bubble falls back to other directions instead of freezing.
details.learning: I learned how inheritance moves shared logic into one place so each subclass only defines what makes it different, and why a class should expose methods instead of letting other code reach into its data. The bubble extension introduced weighted random selection with cumulative probability ranges, and I learned to test randomized behavior with fixed seeds. Working through the diagonal rule and the update order also taught me to trace logic by hand on small examples before trusting it.
